segments.title: The Fog and the Law: Bleak House's Opening Riddle

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, generous, and sometimes heated reading of one of the great novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and today we begin at the beginning — with the fog, the law, and the strange gravitational pull of Dickens's opening chapters.
Bleak House opens with one of the most sustained atmospheric assaults in English prose — fog everywhere, mud everywhere, and the Court of Chancery sitting at the centre of it all.
To help us unpick what Dickens is doing, I'm joined by three remarkable readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that great fiction is finally about moral character — about goodness tested, and sometimes broken, by circumstance.
He reads Dickens with rigour, with affection, and — I should warn you — with occasional scepticism about what he calls over-eager political readings.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows the institutions Dickens depicts from the inside out — what Chancery actually was, what it cost, what it destroyed.
He brings the real world into the room, and he has been known to get genuinely angry about it.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it many times since.
She is our close reader — alert to the verbal music, the comedy, and the moments that make you stop and re-read a sentence.
Let's begin with atmosphere and institution — the two things Dickens locks together from his very first paragraph.
What strikes me, coming back to those opening chapters, is how precisely Dickens understood what Chancery actually was — and how long it could hold a person.
People tend to read the fog as pure metaphor — oppression made visible — but there's something more surgical in the satire.
Dickens catches the system in its holiday, which is almost funnier than catching it at work.
There's a passage in Chapter Nineteen where he describes the Long Vacation — the courts shut, the lawyers scattered across the Continent.
He writes: 'The good ships Law and Equity, those teak-built, copper-bottomed, iron-fastened, brazen-faced, and not by any means fast-sailing clippers are laid up in ordinary.'
That list — teak-built, copper-bottomed, iron-fastened — is pure mock-heroic.
Each adjective adds to the ship's apparent solidity, and then 'brazen-faced' turns the whole thing on its head.
The institution is not slow because it is careful — it is slow because it is shameless.
James is right to savour the rhetoric — that list is genuinely funny — but I want to resist the idea that the satire is simply aimed at an institution.
Dickens is also lampooning the people who feed the institution — who keep it alive through their credulity, their hope, their inability to let go.
The Flying Dutchman image makes this perfectly clear — 'a crew of ghostly clients imploring all whom they may encounter to peruse their papers.'
They are haunting their own lawsuit.
The law has not merely failed them — they have become it.
That is a moral observation as much as a social one, and it is where Dickens's real power lies.
What gets me about that passage — every time — is the rhythm of it.
Teak-built, copper-bottomed, iron-fastened — it's practically iambic.
Dickens is building a ship with his syntax and then sinking it with a single adjective.
And then the Chancery night turns darker when you cross to the Dedlock passages.
There's a Gothic quality to the crippled ancestor's curse that feels almost Jacobean — entirely different register from the satire, and yet it belongs in the same novel.
She drops to the pavement, repulses her husband, and then speaks words you don't forget:
'I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled.'
The repetition of 'I will walk here' — three times — is a spell, almost.
That curse is doing more historical work than it might appear to.
The Dedlock family pride that she invokes is inseparable from the legal and social structures that protected aristocratic property — entails, settlements, the whole apparatus.
And Chancery is part of that apparatus — the court of equity that was supposed to be more humane than common law, and became instead its most elaborate trap.
The line that completes the curse is worth hearing in full:
'And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!'
That word 'disgrace' is precisely calibrated — not merely ruin, but social shame, the undoing of a reputation.
Which is, of course, exactly what the novel will deliver.
I think that passage reveals something James's institutional reading, fine as it is, might underplay.
The woman's silence before the curse is the point — 'she never spoke to any one of being crippled or of being in pain.'
That restraint is a form of pride in itself — not the Dedlock pride she condemns, but something more austere and more admirable.
Dickens is always more interested in how people bear suffering than in the systems that cause it.
That is not a conservative evasion — it is a moral seriousness that political readings too easily flatten.
I take Edmund's point, but I don't think you can have it one way or the other — the suffering and the system are interlocked in Dickens.
There's a passage about the Smallweed family that makes the same argument from pure comedy — and it's almost more devastating for that.
Dickens describes how the Smallweed line has, across generations, 'discarded all amusements, discountenanced all story-books, fairy-tales, fictions, and fables, and banished all levities whatsoever.'
And then the punchline — and it really is a punchline — arrives:

'Hence the gratifying fact that it has had no child born to it and that the complete little men and women whom it has produced have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something depressing on their minds.'
'Gratifying' — that mock-approving word — is doing everything.
The system has produced children who are not children — and Dickens frames it as an achievement.
The Smallweeds are the novel's most concentrated example of what commercial culture does to human development.
Going out early in life, marrying late — that formula is repeated across three generations in the space of one paragraph, almost like a legal precedent being cited.
Each generation reproduces not just its habits but its very physiology — the 'lean and anxious' mind passed down like a bequest.
And yet this family is central to the Jarndyce case — which is to say, the law and the degradation of childhood are not separate themes in this novel.
So we have fog, and law, and a ghostly curse, and children who look like old monkeys — and we're barely past the opening chapters.

What Dickens has done in these early pages is stake out every level of English society — the aristocracy under threat, the law in its holiday complacency, the commercial family grinding its children into premature adulthood.
In our next segment, we'll look at how he keeps all of this in motion — and at the two narrators he uses to hold the whole extraordinary structure together.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme where we read Dickens slowly, carefully, and with the attention he deserves.
I'm joined today by three remarkable readers of this novel, each bringing a very different lens to the text.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Bleak House as a great moral fable about individual character — goodness tested, weakness indulged, self-sacrifice quietly heroic.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — the real institutions, the actual law, the lived experience of poverty and power that Dickens is drawing on.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel who attends above all to what it feels like on the page — the verbal music, the comedy, the moments that make you set the book down and stare at the ceiling.

Today we're looking at character under pressure — specifically, how Dickens uses the people around Richard Carstone to illuminate his slow deterioration, and what that unravelling tells us about the world of the novel.

Edmund, I want to start with you, because before we reach Richard, Dickens gives us two extraordinary portraits of people who manage others without being seen to do so — Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn.
Thank you. What strikes me first about the Lady Dedlock passage is its extraordinary satirical precision — Dickens at his most Swiftian.
Lady Dedlock believes herself to be — Dickens's phrase is quite magnificent here — an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of ordinary mortals.
And yet every tradesman, every dressmaker, every librarian has taken her exact moral measure.
The comparison Dickens reaches for is, I think, one of his great comic images. He tells us that these deferential people lead her and her whole troop after them —
— who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput.
The joke is perfect — the powerful are the tiny ships, and the tradesmen are the giant.
But there is something beneath the comedy — a moral point about how vanity makes one manipulable, how the pretence of power invites the reality of dependence.
What I love about that passage is the sheer relish Dickens takes in the voice of Mr. Sladdery — the repetition of my high connexion, sir, my high connexion — it's almost musical.
And then Dickens delivers the most devastating little aside — in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not exaggerate at all.
That's the sting — honesty in the service of manipulation is still manipulation, and Dickens refuses to let us feel superior to it.
And it connects, I think, directly to Richard — because Richard is equally managed, equally studied, equally unable to see who is reading him.
The Sladdery figure is historically precise — the fashionable circulating library was a genuine institution of social leverage in this period.
Librarians, jewellers, mercers — these were the conduits through which taste was manufactured and sold back to the aristocracy as their own discovery.
Dickens's satirical target is quite precise: a class that believes its preferences are natural, when in fact those preferences are engineered.
Which is exactly what Chancery does to Richard — it engineers his ruin while appearing merely to receive his hope.
Before we reach Richard, I must say a word about Tulkinghorn — because Dickens gives him perhaps the most chilling description in the novel.

He appears at sunset, at his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never slackened — and Dickens tells us that he carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress.
He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress.
Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret.
He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.
He is his own client — that phrase alone is worth several chapters of psychology.
It tells us everything about the peculiar integrity of a man who withholds himself from everyone, including, perhaps, himself.
And Richard is precisely the opposite of Tulkinghorn — where Tulkinghorn withholds everything, Richard conceals nothing, and that openness is what destroys him.
Mrs. Badger sees it plainly. She tells Esther that Richard is of such a very easy disposition that probably he would never think it worth while to mention how he really feels.
He has not that positive interest in it which makes it his vocation. If he has any decided impression in reference to it, I should say it was that it is a tiresome pursuit.
Tiresome. That word does so much work — it's not failure, it's something worse: boredom in the face of duty.
And then Mrs. Badger holds up the contrast — Mr. Woodcourt, who takes medicine from a strong interest in all that it can do.

Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment.
It is a definition of vocation — and Richard has none of it. He is all enthusiasm and no root.
Mrs. Badger's observation is not merely domestic — it maps onto a real Victorian anxiety about young men of middling means and no fixed profession.
The mid-century was full of Richards — men whose expectations exceeded their capacities, who drifted between callings looking for the one that asked nothing difficult of them.
What Chancery does — with devastating efficiency — is give Richard a structure that looks like purpose while actively rewarding idleness and magical thinking.
He doesn't need medicine, or law, or the army — he only needs the suit to come good. And the suit never comes good.
I want to resist, gently, the reading that makes Richard merely a social type.
Because the chapter in which he and Ada declare themselves to Esther is genuinely tender — Dickens gives these young people real feeling.
Esther's account of sitting between them is quite lovely. She says they seemed to have fallen in love with me instead of one another, they were so confiding, and so trustful, and so fond of me.
They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself —
and then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could come to anything.
There is real moral weight here — the word constancy, fortitude, and perseverance placed quietly at the centre — and Richard, at this moment, means every syllable of it.
His tragedy is not that he never loved Ada. His tragedy is that love, even genuine love, could not supply what character could not maintain.
And Mr. Jarndyce sees it — he says so with that characteristic combination of warmth and caution that makes him one of the great English fictional uncles.
He tells Richard: I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here — don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear! — being in a mind to go through life together.
But that was afar off, Rick, afar off.
That repetition — afar off, afar off — it's a warning dressed as a blessing.
Jarndyce can see exactly how young they are, how unformed Richard is — and he is telling him, as kindly as possible, to earn this.
And Richard hears the blessing, not the warning. Which is everything.
The legal dimension of their situation matters here too — Richard and Ada are wards in Chancery, which means their financial futures are literally suspended in the court.
Jarndyce's caution is not merely avuncular sentiment — it has a real legal and economic basis.
These young people cannot marry, cannot settle, cannot plan — because the court has made their futures contingent on a verdict that will not come.
The cruelty of Chancery is not only financial — it is existential. It steals the ability to commit to anything except the suit itself.
And the novel's final word on all of this — on the Gothic atmosphere in which these fates are worked out — comes in one of Esther's most haunting passages.
She is crossing the Thames at night with Bucket in desperate search, and she describes the river in a way that I find genuinely unforgettable.
The river had a fearful look, so overcast and secret, creeping away so fast between the low flat lines of shore —
so heavy with indistinct and awful shapes, both of substance and shadow; so death-like and mysterious.
Substance and shadow — that pairing reaches back through the whole novel.

The world of Bleak House is precisely that — a place where substance and shadow are never quite distinguishable, where what appears solid may dissolve, and what seems like mere atmosphere turns out to be fate.
Substance and shadow — that feels like the right note on which to close this part of our conversation.
We've moved from Lady Dedlock's drawing room to the dark Thames, and somewhere between the two, Richard Carstone has lost his footing — and Dickens has shown us, step by careful step, exactly how.
My thanks to Edmund, James, and Caroline — and we'll continue with the next dimension of the novel in just a moment.

segments.title: A Woman's Secret, A Nation's Justice

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we are inside what I think is the most quietly terrifying dynamic in the novel — the slow, watchful war between Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn.
A secret buried for decades, a lawyer who knows how to wait, and a woman who has learned to wear composure like armour.
With me today are Edmund Leigh, whose moral imagination is well-matched to the moral peril at the heart of this story.
James Blackstone, who will keep us honest about what the law actually was and what it actually did to people.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who reads Dickens with the kind of attention that makes you want to go back to the book immediately.
Let's begin with the moment the secret starts to move — Tulkinghorn's message, delivered via Sir Leicester, almost absently, almost as an afterthought.
What strikes me every time I read that scene is the sheer cruelty of the delivery mechanism.
Tulkinghorn doesn't come to Lady Dedlock directly — he routes his message through her husband, who fumbles with his eye-glass and loses his place in the letter.
And then Sir Leicester finally finds the passage and reads it aloud — and it lands like a trap sprung in a drawing room.
The words are these — and listen to how measured they are:
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Three words at the end. I have seen him.
Tulkinghorn doesn't need to say more. He knows exactly how much rope to give her.
The rope metaphor is apt, and I'd press it a little further.
Tulkinghorn doesn't give Lady Dedlock rope to hang herself — he gives her rope to feel the noose, and then waits to see whether she will pull.
That is a portrait of a certain kind of moral ugliness — not passion, not even malice in any warm sense, but cold custodianship of another's ruin.
And what Dickens shows us in the scene that follows is that Lady Dedlock recognises this completely — and matches it.
There is a passage — devastating in its restraint — that describes their subsequent meetings at Chesney Wold.
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
That phrase — exhausted deity — is one of the most perfectly compressed character descriptions in the English novel.
She has made herself into an object of worship, and it has cost her everything human.
I want to hold Edmund's point about custodianship and bring it into focus, because what Tulkinghorn represents institutionally is quite precise.
He is a solicitor in private practice whose entire professional identity rests on holding the secrets of great families — that was the actual structure of the Victorian legal world.
He is not employed by the law courts — he is employed by the Dedlocks — and that distinction matters enormously for understanding what kind of power he wields.
Dickens catches this perfectly in that phrase — "the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home."
Out of place socially — he is not gentry — but at home in every room because he knows what every room conceals.
That is the precise anatomy of a certain professional power that existed then and — I will not labour the point — exists in recognisable form today.
What moves me — and unnerves me — in these passages is the mutual surveillance Dickens describes.
These two people are watching each other constantly, and yet to all outward appearances, they take almost no notice of each other whatsoever.
And then Dickens gives us this extraordinary passage — I never tire of it:

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
That word evermore, repeated three times — it has a toll like a bell.
It is not suspense in any thriller sense — it is the sustained, exhausting vigilance of two people who cannot afford a single unguarded moment.
One observation about Sir Leicester in these scenes, which I think tends to be overlooked.
While his wife and his lawyer conduct their silent duel, Dickens tells us he looks at the fire — with, and this is the phrase, "the general expression of the Dedlock on the staircase."
That is to say, he wears the ancestral blankness — the settled, hereditary incuriosity of his class.
Now one could read that as Dickens mocking him — and certainly there is mockery in it.
But I would argue it also functions as a kind of terrible irony — because his very obliviousness is what permits the catastrophe that is building around him.
He trusts — and Dickens shows us this explicitly — that no association in Lady Dedlock's mind could possibly connect to a person of such low station.
His rank, which he believes protects him, is precisely the blindfold he cannot remove.
That connects very directly to something Dickens builds across the whole novel — the way secrets are not just personal but structural.
We learn from Mr. Jarndyce that the lady who arranged Esther's upbringing refused to disclose her identity under any circumstances whatsoever.
The phrasing Jarndyce uses is exact — and worth attending to:
"That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
For any human consideration. That is an absolute.
And what we understand, reading on, is that her resolution is not merely pride — it is the survival strategy of a woman who has no legal recourse, no formal protection, nothing but concealment.
The law that Tulkinghorn wields is precisely the law that offers her nothing — and she knows it.
And this is where Chancery becomes not a background institution but an active destroyer of human connection.
There is a moment — Esther reporting Gridley's words near the end of Chapter Twenty-four — that makes this shatteringly clear.
Gridley is dying and he says — and Esther hears these words echoing through Richard's departure too:
"Of all my old associations, of all my old pursuits and hopes, of all the living and the dead world, this one poor soul alone comes natural to me, and I am fit for.
There is a tie of many suffering years between us two, and it is the only tie I ever had on earth that Chancery has not broken!"
The only tie Chancery has not broken. Every other bond — family, hope, labour, love — gone.
And this is why Lady Dedlock's secret is not merely a plot device — it lives inside the same world of institutional destruction that Gridley dies inside.
Caroline makes a connection I feel is quite profound — and I want to gently qualify it, because I think Dickens is doing something even more unsettling than institutional critique.
Gridley's cry is powerful — but it is the cry of a man who has allowed an institution to consume his entire self.
Lady Dedlock, by contrast, has done something different — she has enclosed her secret so completely that she has become the performance.
That is not institutional damage — that is a freely chosen strategy that has exacted a terrible personal cost.
And Dickens, I believe, asks us to hold both — the systemic destruction and the individual moral choice — without collapsing one into the other.
I don't dispute that — but I'd say the distinction between chosen strategy and institutional constraint was considerably narrower for a woman in Lady Dedlock's position than Edmund implies.
What choices, precisely, did she have?
The law gave her none. Society gave her the performance or the abyss.

Dickens understood that — and the novel's sympathy for her, I think, is entirely consistent with recognising that the performance was not a failure of character but a response to an impossible situation.
Which is perhaps why that mutual watching — that word evermore — feels so tragic rather than merely theatrical.
Two people locked in a contest neither can afford to lose, over a secret that, once broken, will cost one of them everything.
We'll return in a moment to look at what that secret means for Esther — who stands at the centre of it, without yet knowing she is there.

segments.title: The Boy Nobody Sees: Jo and the Machinery of Cruelty

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel seriously — one passage, one argument, one revelation at a time.
Today we're looking at one of the novel's most uncomfortable chapters — the inquest into the death of Nemo, the anonymous law-writer found dead in his garret.
What the inquest reveals, above all, is a boy called Jo — a crossing-sweeper who barely exists in the eyes of the law, and yet carries the novel's moral weight on his thin shoulders.
With me today are three readers who know this novel intimately and see it very differently.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Bleak House as a great moral story about individual character — and who keeps the rest of us honest when we reach for easy political conclusions.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what these institutions were, how they worked, and who they crushed.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of classic fiction, who comes to this chapter not as a scholar but as someone who has wept over it more than once.
Let's begin with Jo in the witness box — or rather, not in it, because the court won't have him.
What stops me every single time I read the testimony passage is its form — the syntax itself.
Dickens strips Jo down to fragments — no conjunctions, no connective tissue — just bare declarative facts, one after another.
Listen to how it accumulates.
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Three negatives, each one a door closed, and then the fourth — school — which isn't even framed as a loss, just an absence.
Jo doesn't grieve what he's never had. That's almost the most terrible thing about it.
And then Dickens gives him something extraordinary — a moral sense that arrived from nowhere.
"Knows a broom's a broom, and knows it's wicked to tell a lie. Don't recollect who told him about the broom or about the lie, but knows both."
He knows the practical and the ethical — broom and lie — with equal certainty and equal mystery about where either came from.
Caroline is quite right to dwell on the syntax, and I would go further.
What Dickens has achieved here is a portrait of natural moral intuition — conscience without catechism, as it were.
This is not primarily an indictment of institutions. It is something far more interesting.
It is Dickens asking: what remains of a human being when everything society might offer has been withheld?
And his answer is — character persists. A kind of irreducible moral kernel survives.
The passage about the dead man — Nemo — reinforces this beautifully.
The narrator turns directly to Jo and says — and one must quote this properly —
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
A ray of light — not a flood, not a redemption — merely a distant ray.
Dickens is precise in his mercy. He does not sentimentalise Jo's condition; he honours it.
Edmund's reading is generous to Dickens, and in many ways correct — but I think we cannot entirely separate the individual portrait from its institutional context.
Jo is not simply a child without family. He is a child the legal machinery has positively excluded.
The coroner's inquest was a formal legal proceeding, and witnesses were required to understand the oath — its religious and legal force.
Jo cannot swear because he doesn't know what swearing means in that context. So he is rejected as incompetent.
What Dickens shows us is a system that first denies Jo any education, then uses his resulting ignorance to deny him a legal voice.
The circularity is the cruelty. It is not accidental — it is structural.
And the contrast with Mrs. Piper's testimony is almost savage in its comedy.
She is allowed to speak at extraordinary length, producing almost nothing of substance.
"Why, Mrs. Piper has a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
She has legal standing. Her testimony is worthless. Jo has genuine knowledge and genuine feeling, and he is turned away at the door.
That contrast is devastating when you read the two passages side by side — which is what Dickens intends.
Mrs. Piper's speech is a masterpiece of comic prose — and I don't mean that dismissively.
The breathless unpunctuation, the nested parentheses about baby Alexander James Piper aged eighteen months and four days — Dickens is having tremendous fun here.
But that fun is doing serious work. Because while we're laughing at Mrs. Piper's vapid testimony, we feel the injustice of Jo's exclusion all the more sharply.
And then there's the moment the narrator addresses Jo directly — by name, in the second person.
"Jo, is it thou?" — that biblical "thou" — the narrator sees Jo even when the law refuses to.
And what breaks my heart is that the ray of light — the tiny grace — comes from Jo's own loyalty.
He loved the dead man. That is all. That is the whole of his testimony, the whole of his case for existing.
I find I cannot disagree with Caroline's reading of the narrator's address — and I say that as someone who distrusts sentimentality in criticism almost as much as in life.
The "thou" is precisely chosen — archaic, scriptural, intimate.
It removes Jo from the secular proceedings of the coroner's court and places him in a different jurisdiction altogether.
Though I would note — James is correct that the indictment of the legal system is real — what makes it powerful is that Dickens never lets the system become the whole story.
Jo matters not because he is a victim of Chancery but because he is, in some irreducible sense, a person.
And that distinction — between person and case — is precisely where Dickens is most modern and most radical.
The system sees Jo as neither plaintiff nor witness. He occupies no legal category that grants him standing.
And yet Dickens constructs the chapter so that Jo's three-sentence self-portrait is the most morally coherent testimony in the room.
Consider what he actually says about death and punishment — the novel renders his dialect faithfully.

"Can't exactly say what'll be done to him arter he's dead if he tells a lie to the gentlemen here, but believes it'll be something wery bad to punish him, and serve him right—and so he'll tell the truth."
He doesn't know the theology. But he knows that lying to those men would be wrong, and that the consequences would be deserved.
That is a more rigorous moral conscience than most of what the court contains.
And Dickens doesn't let the novel forget Jo — this chapter plants a seed that grows darker with every reappearance.
The machinery of cruelty that excludes Jo here will eventually move against him with far greater force — and against those around him.
In our next segment, we look at that machinery in motion — Mr. Bucket, a woman in flight, and whether detection is a form of rescue or a form of pursuit.

segments.title: Reading Dickens Aloud: Where the Novel's Heart Beats

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme where we take one of the great Victorian novels apart — sentence by sentence, if necessary — to understand why it still grips us.
I'm joined today by three people who love this book with the kind of love that demands argument.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don, a man who believes the novel's genius lies in moral imagination and individual character — not in social programme.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who can tell you exactly what Chancery was, what it cost people, and why it mattered.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has been re-reading it ever since — with particular attention to where it sings.
Today's segment is about reading Dickens aloud — where the novel's heart actually beats.
Caroline, you've been the one in this group most willing to read passages out loud. Where do you want us to start?
I want to start with a moment that has haunted me since the first time I read it.
It's early in the novel — Esther, Ada, and Richard encounter an old woman outside the Court of Chancery.
Richard has made some thoughtless remark implying she might be mad, and she turns on him — swiftly, precisely, terribly.
She says she was a Chancery ward herself — that she once had youth, hope, beauty.
"Neither of the three served or saved me. I have the honour to attend court regularly. With my documents. I expect a judgment. Shortly. On the Day of Judgment."
Those short sentences land like blows. Dickens lets her speak in fragments — each one a small door closing.
And then she tips into something that sounds like madness — the sixth seal, the Great Seal — and then offers her blessing.
You cannot laugh. You cannot quite weep. You can only read it again.
Caroline is quite right to stop there — though I'd resist the word 'haunted,' which is too comfortable a word for what Dickens does.
What is extraordinary about that passage is its moral precision.
The woman curtsies and smiles between every little sentence — Dickens notes that — and the contrast between her courtesy and her content is devastating.
She is not raving. She is performing the social forms that Chancery has taught her, even as Chancery has destroyed her.
That is Dickens the moralist at his finest — not the polemicist, the moralist.
Edmund's distinction is fair, though I think you can be a moralist and a polemicist at the same moment — and Dickens frequently was.
What that passage captures with historical accuracy is that Chancery wards were real people — caught for decades in genuine legal limbo, their estates consumed in costs.
The woman's expectation of a judgment — "shortly" — is not madness invented for effect.
It mirrors the delusional hope that real Chancery litigants maintained, sometimes across generations.
The Day of Judgment as a legal deadline is a joke, yes — but it's a joke with a precise historical target.
And then Dickens turns this entirely on its head later in the novel, with Vholes.
Where the old woman's tragedy is raw and unguarded, Vholes is all professional surface — perfectly calibrated repulsiveness.
There's a passage where he discusses Ada — this is the woman Richard has secretly married — and Vholes describes her eligibility.
"I dare say the young lady is equally eligible in that point of view. She is considered so (I have heard) among the clerks in the Inn, and it is a point more in their way than in mine."
The comedy is in that parenthetical — 'I have heard.' As if beauty were a legal precedent he has noted but not verified.
He cannot be a judge of beauty. He has never, from a boy, given much attention to it.
And yet he can tell you what the clerks at the Inn think. The detail is immaculate.
Vholes is one of Dickens's finest comic-sinister creations, and it is Caroline's point about detail that I would underline.
Vholes never loses his professional composure. That is precisely what makes him monstrous.
He is not corrupt in any lurid sense. He is merely entirely indifferent to human beings while maintaining every form of respect for them.
Burke would have recognised that type. An institution that has outrun its own moral purpose, preserved in the amber of professional habit.
The clerks at the Inn as arbiters of female beauty — that line is worth dwelling on.
It locates Ada's value entirely within the legal world's social economy — she is eligible, she is genteel, she is considered so.
Her own feelings, her own tragedy, are invisible to Vholes — as invisible as the old woman's hope was to Chancery itself.
Dickens is consistent in this: the institution sees only what the institution needs to see.
And then there's Bucket — who is in a completely different register from either of those.
Bucket has a scene late in the novel where he's manoeuvring old Smallweed into revealing a hidden document.
It is pure theatre. Bucket leads Smallweed through the disclosure with this air of cheerful raillery — Dickens's own phrase.
He says, stooping over the old man:
"And so you chance to find, you know, a paper with the signature of Jarndyce to it. Don't you?"
It sounds like a friendly reminiscence — as if they're sharing a joke about something that happened to someone else.
And then the reveal — the paper is a will.
"What do you find it to be but a will, you see. That's the drollery of it."
'The drollery of it.' Bucket is genuinely delighted. Smallweed, of course, is not.
What's legally significant there is that a later will — if it is later — could overturn the entire Jarndyce and Jarndyce settlement.
And Bucket knows this. He's not just enjoying the scene — though he clearly is — he is managing it with complete tactical precision.
'Drollery' is exactly the right word for Bucket's performance — it's dry, it's controlled, and it conceals the stakes entirely.
Bucket is, in one sense, the novel's great pragmatist — a man who works within the systems that destroy other characters, and is not destroyed.
And what Caroline's reading captures is that his comedy is inseparable from his competence.
He is funny precisely because he is formidable. The raillery is the method, not the mask.
What strikes me listening to all three of those passages together is how different the comedy is in each one — and yet how connected.
The old woman's dark wit, Vholes's impeccable blankness, Bucket's performative geniality — they're all Dickens, but they couldn't be more unlike each other.
That range is part of what makes reading this novel aloud such a particular pleasure — and such a demand.
We'll carry some of these threads forward as we move to our next discussion. Stay with us.

segments.title: Moral Imagination Against the System: What Bleak House Insists We See

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great novel apart — slowly, carefully, with the respect it deserves.
I'm your host, and today we're asking what the novel insists we see — morally, politically, and above all, humanly.
With me today are three guests who know this book intimately and disagree about it in the most productive ways.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that great novels are finally about individual character — goodness tested, will weakened, conscience questioned.
He reads Bleak House with a critic's eye for moral imagination, and he's suspicious of readings that reduce Dickens to a pamphleteer.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what Chancery was, what it cost, and who paid.
He brings the institutions alive — not as background colour, but as forces that shaped real lives.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has never quite recovered.
She focuses on what it feels like to read the novel — the sentences that stop you cold, the characters who refuse to leave.
Edmund, let's begin with the novel's opening — because Dickens does something extraordinary before he introduces a single character.
He announces a world.
And what a world it is — not yet populated with people, but already saturated with moral atmosphere.
The prose itself is extraordinary.
Listen to this.

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
That is not social commentary in any narrow sense.
That is a mythological act — Dickens reaches back before human history and asks what creature this city resembles.
The Megalosaurus is not a metaphor for capitalism.
It is an image of primal, unreclaimed disorder — the world before conscience, before form.
I take Edmund's point about the mythological register, and I don't entirely dispute it.
But I'd want to note that the disorder Dickens conjures is not ahistorical — it has a very specific institutional address.
The fog descends, and immediately we are told the Lord Chancellor is sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall.
The atmosphere and the institution are one.
And later the novel will tell us directly what the institution is for.
"The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself."
That sentence is not gothic atmosphere — it is a diagnosis.
And the clinical precision of it is what makes it devastating, in a way that the fog, for all its beauty, cannot quite achieve.
The precision is admirable, I grant you.
But a diagnosis without a patient is merely clever.
What gives the novel its permanent force is not the exposure of Chancery — Chancery was reformed before the book was even finished — but the human beings caught inside it.
And the human being who haunts me most — who I think proves my case absolutely — is Jo.
There is a passage where Jo is weeping for a man he barely knew — a man who was kind to him.
"He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
No system is being satirised there.
What we encounter is gratitude — the purest form of it — expressed in the most broken of accents.
That is what Dickens's moral imagination insists we see: not the maze, but the child inside it.
I think Edmund is right that Jo breaks you open in a way no satirical paragraph can.
But I'd want to push back slightly on the idea that these two modes — the systemic and the personal — are in competition.
What makes Jo's grief so unbearable is that we already know — the novel has made us know — that nothing will be done for him.
The personal and the systemic are not alternatives in Bleak House.
They are held in terrible tension on every page.
And I notice the spelling — 'wery', 'wos' — the non-standard orthography Dickens uses for Jo.
It doesn't condescend — it insists on the particularity of this voice, this child, this sorrow.
You cannot universalise him away.
That word — 'universalise' — is exactly right.
The institutions in this novel depend on abstraction.
They depend on the individual case disappearing into process.
Look at what Bucket does with Jo — and it's rendered with such cold precision.
"Bucket stealthily tells the coins from one hand into the other like counters — which is a way he has, his principal use of them being in these games of skill."
'Games of skill.' That phrase does a great deal of quiet damage.
People are counters in this system — Jo most of all.
And Bucket, who is brilliant, is himself an instrument of a larger mechanism he doesn't question.
I wouldn't quarrel with the observation about Bucket — it's acute.
Though I'd note that Dickens doesn't condemn Bucket entirely — he allows him a kind of professional grace.
But your phrase 'instrument of a mechanism' — that, I think, is the novel's deepest fear.
Not that wicked men run wicked institutions — but that ordinary men run them so very competently.
And meanwhile the fog continues.
That opening — the sun in mourning, the soot like snowflakes — it doesn't resolve.
Dickens writes 'gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun' — and I find that phrase genuinely frightening.
"Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown snowflakes — gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun."
The sun is not obscured — it is dead.
That is not satire.
That is elegy — for something the novel suspects may already be lost before the story has even begun.
Elegy, diagnosis, myth — this novel refuses to be pinned to a single register.
And I think that refusal is itself part of the argument Bleak House is making.
We'll return to what that argument demands of us as readers — and what it costs us to truly look at what Dickens is showing.

segments.title: Law's Theatre: Jarndyce and Jarndyce as the Novel's True Character

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been circling the great fog-machine at the heart of the novel — the Court of Chancery, and the case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
This segment, we want to examine what the law actually does in Bleak House — not just as backdrop, but as a kind of character in its own right.
James Blackstone has been waiting, I suspect, for precisely this conversation.
James — you bring the historian's eye to what Dickens actually got right, and what he exaggerated, about Victorian legal institutions.
Edmund Leigh is with us as well — Edmund, whose instinct is always to ask whether Dickens is writing a social tract or a moral fable.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who I suspect will bring us back to the actual sentences on the page whenever we drift too far into abstraction.
James, let's begin with you.
Thank you.
What Dickens understood — and I mean understood with genuine precision — is that the law's great vice is not malice but institutional momentum.
No one in Chancery is twirling a moustache.
They are all simply doing what the system rewards them for doing.
The Vholes passage is, for my money, the sharpest piece of institutional satire in Victorian fiction.
Dickens stages it as a mock parliamentary inquiry, and the comedy is absolutely merciless.
Mr. Kenge is given this extraordinary speech to a client who dares suggest reform.
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
And the threat is not to justice, or to the client's interests — it is to Vholes's respectability.
That word — respectability — does all the work that logic refuses to do.
I won't dispute that the satire is precise.
But I'd want to separate two things: the satirical machinery, which is brilliant, and the claim that this is primarily a novel about institutions.
Dickens is interested in what Chancery does to particular souls.
Not to a class, not to a system — to Richard Carstone, to Miss Flite, to John Jarndyce himself.
The Tulkinghorn passage James might turn to is instructive on that point.
Because there, the exercise of power is intensely, almost claustrophobically personal.
Tulkinghorn doesn't invoke the system — he invokes the alarm-bell.
He says, with perfect calm, that before Lady Dedlock reaches the staircase — and I think the theatrical precision of that phrase is deliberate —
"before you reach the staircase I shall ring the alarm-bell and rouse the house."
The law here is not an institution grinding on in the background — it is one cold man in a room.
Both of those passages are devastating, and in such different registers.
The Vholes satire has this almost gleeful quality — you feel Dickens enjoying himself enormously.
The Tulkinghorn scene is something else entirely — it's cold, it's Gothic, it's terrifying.
What strikes me is the detail that Tulkinghorn doesn't stir hand or foot.
He doesn't need to move.
Power that doesn't need to move is somehow the most frightening kind.
And then you set that beside what Esther sees in those two beaten women — coarse, shabby, united.
Esther has this line that I find quietly extraordinary.
"What the poor are to the poor is little known, excepting to themselves and God."
It's not angry — it's almost a whisper.
But it contains a more radical indictment of class than ten pamphlets.
That passage from Esther is one I return to often, precisely because it refuses the consolations of either anger or sentimentality.
It names something true about the structural invisibility of the poor to reformers, philanthropists — even well-meaning observers.
Which brings me to Mrs. Jellyby — and that extraordinary moment when her husband finally speaks.
Mr. Jellyby has been a figure of gentle comic ruin throughout the novel — head against the wall, speechless.
And then he gives his daughter the only piece of counsel in the entire book that is both entirely sincere and entirely devastating.
"Never have a mission, my dear child."
Five words.
A whole critique of abstracted benevolence — and of Mrs. Jellyby's brand of it in particular — compressed into five words.
James is quite right that those five words do enormous work.
And I'd argue they are doing something morally precise, not politically convenient.
Mrs. Jellyby's failure is not that she cares about Africa — it is that she has made caring into a substitute for seeing.
That is a failure of character, not merely of policy.
And notice that it takes the broken, ruined husband — not the eloquent Esther, not the sensible Jarndyce — to say it plainly.
Dickens has a great gift for placing moral truth in unexpected mouths.
And the Rouncewell passage, I think, is where all of these threads — law, class, duty, the invisible lives of servants — come together most painfully.
Mrs. Rouncewell is pleading with Lady Dedlock to help clear her son.
And she does it with this devastating, clear-eyed acknowledgement of the distance between them.
She says, and I have to read this in full —

"My Lady, you may have some proud or angry reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray, oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been passed in this family which she dearly loves."
The double 'pray' — she can't help herself.
It's not rhetorical — it's a woman at the limit of what language can do.
And the narrator's comment — 'the old housekeeper pleads with genuine simplicity' — is Dickens holding his own prose to account.
What Caroline identifies there is something crucial about how power operates in this novel — it is always gendered, always classed, and always enacted at the level of the body and the voice.
Mrs. Rouncewell has to make herself small to be heard.
Lady Dedlock has to remain silent to survive.
And Tulkinghorn needs only to not move.
The distribution of stillness in this novel is a map of power.
I find that a remarkably fine formulation.
Though I'd add that Dickens does not leave us without counter-examples.
Esther moves through the novel doing things — small, continuous, unglamorous things.
Mrs. Rouncewell's act of kneeling to plead is itself a form of power — the power of a woman who knows exactly what she is asking and why.
Dickens never argues that individuals are helpless before institutions.
He argues that the cost of resisting them is paid in flesh and spirit.
That feels like a genuinely useful distinction to carry into the rest of the episode.
The law as grinding system; power as enacted in individual bodies; and the cost measured in those bodies.
We'll be turning next to the question of narration — why Dickens gave us two voices to tell this story, and what the doubling does.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Lives We Almost Lose Track Of: What Endures After Bleak House

utterances.text: We've arrived at the end of our journey through Bleak House — or rather, at the place where the novel asks us to look back.
Because this is a novel that has endings built into its very middle — moments where Dickens pauses the machinery of plot and asks what will become of these young lives.
The passages before us all come from Chapter Thirteen — Mr. Jarndyce's counsel to Richard and Ada, and Esther's extraordinary final image of them walking out of the sunlight.
Edmund, James, Caroline — I want to ask each of you: what do these pages leave you with, as readers, as thinkers, as people who have spent time inside this novel?
What strikes me first — and most forcibly — is the sheer moral generosity of Jarndyce in these pages.
He is a man who might very easily have played the patriarch — who might have leveraged his guardianship into control.
Instead, he does something far rarer and far harder.
He grants them the freedom to change — and assures them that change will not cost them his love.
He frames it like this — and I do want the words themselves to be heard:

"if you DO change — if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl — don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
Nothing monstrous or uncommon — that is a phrase worth sitting with.
Dickens, through Jarndyce, is doing something Johnson would have recognised: insisting that ordinary human frailty is not a moral catastrophe.
Edmund's point about generosity is well taken — but I'd press on it slightly.
Jarndyce tells them he has no power over them — and technically, in law, that is increasingly true as they approach adulthood.
But the emotional power he holds is enormous — and Dickens knows it.
What interests me in the second passage is the counsel about effort — the extraordinary specificity of it.
Jarndyce says to Richard:
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
The heathen waggoner — that's a biblical allusion, the man who prays to Hercules without putting his shoulder to the wheel.
Jarndyce is warning Richard, with real urgency, that faith alone — even faith in love — accomplishes nothing without sustained application.
We, as readers, already know Richard will not heed this. That is precisely what makes it so painful.
James has named the ache of it — we know Richard won't listen.
But what Dickens does at the end of this chapter is something else entirely — something that works on the reader almost beneath the level of argument.
Esther watches them leave. That's all. She simply watches.
And then she gives us this — I've read it probably thirty times and it still stops me:

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness.
So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
"The room darkened as they went out" — Dickens doesn't explain that.
He doesn't need to. The weather does the work. The syntax does the work. That word "lightly" — and then the shadow.
Caroline has identified something essential — the passage works because Dickens keeps Esther's own emotion almost entirely out of it.
She reports what she sees. The clouding over is literal — or so we are permitted to believe for a moment.
And yet the rhythm of the sentences — "so young, so beautiful, so full" — that triple cadence is anything but neutral reportage.
It has the weight of an elegy. Dickens is already mourning them while they are still walking out of the room.
And that is, I think, what makes Bleak House so different from a simple indictment of institutions.
The Chancery suit will eventually consume Richard — that is the novel's great structural tragedy.
But Jarndyce's warning is not about the law. It is about character — about what Richard chooses to do with his own will.
He tells Richard that success in great things or small "could be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts" — and the answer is it cannot.
The system is culpable. But so, in the end, is Richard. Dickens insists on holding both truths.
What I keep returning to is the phrase Jarndyce uses — "leave your cousin Ada here."
It's the sharpest thing he says. Softer than a threat, harder than a plea.
And Ada, in that final image, looking up at Richard's face — she sees nothing else.
That is the heartbreak the novel stores up for us. She loves him entirely. And he is already half-lost.
Edmund, James, Caroline — I think you've done something that Bleak House itself does so well: held the tenderness and the foreboding in the same breath.
A young man and a young woman, walking through the sunlight into the shadow — and a guardian who gave them every wise word he had, knowing they might not hear it.
That is the particular gift of this novel — that it can make us grieve for what hasn't happened yet, on the very page where hope is still intact.
Thank you all for being such generous and perceptive company through Bleak House Unpacked.
And thank you, most of all, to you for listening — for giving your time to this great, dark, inexhaustible novel.

c19:p0.text:
It is the long vacation in the regions of Chancery Lane. The good
ships Law and Equity, those teak-built, copper-bottomed,
iron-fastened, brazen-faced, and not by any means fast-sailing
clippers are laid up in ordinary. The Flying Dutchman, with a crew of
ghostly clients imploring all whom they may encounter to peruse their
papers, has drifted, for the time being, heaven knows where. The
courts are all shut up; the public offices lie in a hot sleep.
Westminster Hall itself is a shady solitude where nightingales might
sing, and a tenderer class of suitors than is usually found there,
walk.
c19:p0.summary: During the long vacation, the legal profession is dormant; the courts, offices, and Westminster Hall are empty as lawyers and clerks scatter across the continent.
c19:p0.best_quote: The good ships Law and Equity, those teak-built, copper-bottomed, iron-fastened, brazen-faced, and not by any means fast-sailing clippers are laid up in ordinary.

c7:p59.text:
“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”
c7:p59.summary: The crippled lady, after her husband finds her on the pavement, looks at him coldly and curses the Dedlock family: she will walk the terrace forever as a warning of coming calamity and disgrace.
c7:p59.best_quote: I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!

c21:p4.text:
His spirit shone through his son, to whom he had always preached of
“going out” early in life and whom he made a clerk in a sharp
scrivener’s office at twelve years old. There the young gentleman
improved his mind, which was of a lean and anxious character, and
developing the family gifts, gradually elevated himself into the
discounting profession. Going out early in life and marrying late, as
his father had done before him, he too begat a lean and
anxious-minded son, who in his turn, going out early in life and
marrying late, became the father of Bartholomew and Judith Smallweed,
twins. During the whole time consumed in the slow growth of this
family tree, the house of Smallweed, always early to go out and late
to marry, has strengthened itself in its practical character, has
discarded all amusements, discountenanced all story-books,
fairy-tales, fictions, and fables, and banished all levities
whatsoever. Hence the gratifying fact that it has had no child born
to it and that the complete little men and women whom it has produced
have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something
depressing on their minds.
c21:p4.summary: The narrator traces how successive Smallweed generations have perpetuated a culture of early entry into commerce and late marriage, deliberately eliminating all levity and amusement, producing stunted premature adults.
c21:p4.best_quote: Hence the gratifying fact that it has had no child born to it and that the complete little men and women whom it has produced have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something depressing on their minds.

c2:p12.text:
Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.
c2:p12.summary: Despite believing herself inscrutable, Lady Dedlock is perfectly understood and managed by tradespeople and servants who deliberately lead her and her circle by flattery and careful study of her preferences.
c2:p12.best_quote: who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput

c12:p67.text:
At length, one afternoon a little before sunset, when the bright
groups of figures which have for the last hour or two enlivened the
Ghost’s Walk are all dispersed and only Sir Leicester and my Lady
remain upon the terrace, Mr. Tulkinghorn appears. He comes towards
them at his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never
slackened. He wears his usual expressionless mask—if it be a
mask—and carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every
crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great
or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his
personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients;
he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.
c12:p67.summary: At sunset, Tulkinghorn finally appears, moving at his usual methodical pace with an expressionless mask, embodying mystery and unknown knowledge.
c12:p67.best_quote: He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.

c17:p19.text:
“My dear Miss Summerson,” she replied, “on Mr. Carstone’s character
and conduct. He is of such a very easy disposition that probably he
would never think it worth while to mention how he really feels, but
he feels languid about the profession. He has not that positive
interest in it which makes it his vocation. If he has any decided
impression in reference to it, I should say it was that it is a
tiresome pursuit. Now, this is not promising. Young men like Mr.
Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can
do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a
very little money and through years of considerable endurance and
disappointment. But I am quite convinced that this would never be the
case with Mr. Carstone.”
c17:p19.summary: Mrs. Badger elaborates that Richard lacks the positive interest in medicine that sustains practitioners through hardship, unlike Mr. Woodcourt whose commitment comes from genuine passion.
c17:p19.best_quote: Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment.

c13:p99.text:
There he was, of course. They brought a chair on either side of me,
and put me between them, and really seemed to have fallen in love
with me instead of one another, they were so confiding, and so
trustful, and so fond of me. They went on in their own wild way for a
little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and
then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how
there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said
that he would work his fingers to the bone for Ada, and Ada said that
she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,
advising and talking, half the night. Finally, before we parted, I
gave them my promise to speak to their cousin John to-morrow.

face that made my heart die within me. The river had a fearful look,

lines of shore—so heavy with indistinct and awful shapes, both of
substance and shadow; so death-like and mysterious. I have seen it

the bridge are always burning dim, the cutting wind is eddying round

London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.

c13:p124.summary: As Ada and Richard leave, Esther observes them passing through sunlit rooms, young and full of hope, but the sun clouds over as they depart, suggesting a foreboding shadow.
c13:p124.best_quote: So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness. So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over.

c13:p115.text:
“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”
c13:p115.summary: Mr. Jarndyce counsels Ada and Richard that while he assumes their love will endure, if they change he will remain their confidant and will not judge them.

All I say before speaking to you according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me, Rick!)—don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it.

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”
c13:p118.summary: Mr. Jarndyce advises Richard to trust Providence and his own efforts equally, to combine constancy in love with diligent effort in all pursuits, and never to expect success without genuine commitment.
